definition: The study of alignments of random points in a plane seeks to discover subsets of points that occupy an approximately straight line within a larger set of points that are randomly placed in a planar region.
details: Studies have shown that such near-alignments occur by chance with greater frequency than one might intuitively expect. This has been put forward as a demonstration that ley lines and other similar mysterious alignments believed by some to be phenomena of deep significance might exist solely due to chance alone, as opposed to the supernatural or anthropological explanations put forward by their proponents. The topic has also been studied in the fields of computer vision and astronomy. A number of studies have examined the mathematics of alignment of random points on the plane. In all of these, the width of the line — the allowed displacement of the positions of the points from a perfect straight line — is important. It allows the fact that real-world features are not mathematical points, and that their positions need not line up exactly for them to be considered in alignment. Alfred Watkins, in his classic work on ley lines The Old Straight Track, used the width of a pencil line on a map as the threshold for the tolerance of what might be regarded as an alignment. explainer.lead: Randomly scattered points often form surprisingly convincing near-straight lines simply by chance. Studying when and how often this happens helps distinguish an unusual pattern from one that needs no deliberate or mysterious explanation.

tiers.eli5: Scatter a handful of buttons on the floor and look for several that almost form a straight row. With enough buttons, and a generous enough idea of “almost”, you will find rows even though nobody arranged them. That is why a surprising line on a map is not automatically evidence that someone planned it.
tiers.practitioner: In computer vision or astronomy, chance alignment provides a baseline before near-collinear detections are interpreted as meaningful structure. Set the number of points k, tolerance width w, and search region explicitly; real detections need only fall within w/2 of some line. Counts are highly sensitive to w and grow combinatorially with n and area, while boundary losses require an edge-effect correction in the three-point estimate.
tiers.paperLevel: For n points in a compact planar region of approximate diameter L, a k-point alignment is a subset contained in at least one straight path of width w. Under approximately uniform placement, with w << L, a rough expected count is C(n,k)(w/L)^(k-2). For three-point alignments of maximum length d in a square of side L, mu = (pi/3)(w/L)(d/L)^3 n(n-1)(n-2), ignoring edge effects; boundary losses add a correction term.

explainer.example: On a 1:50,000 Ordnance Survey map, Alfred Watkins’s 1 mm pencil-line tolerance corresponds to a 50 m-wide path on the ground. Several randomly positioned landmarks anywhere inside that corridor count as aligned, even though their positions do not sit exactly on one mathematical line.

explainer.intuition: Any particular group of points is unlikely to line up, but a larger collection creates vastly more groups to try. That combinatorial growth can overwhelm the falling probability for each group, especially when “aligned” allows a nonzero tolerance.
howItWorks: Start with n points scattered across a planar region of approximate diameter L.
Choose a subset of k points that might form a line.
Allow a track of width w: every point must lie within distance w/2 of some straight line.
Repeat the test across possible subsets and count the qualifying alignments.
Estimate chance expectations using the number of subsets and the tolerance ratio w/L.
explainer.whyItMatters: The idea shows why ley lines and similar patterns can arise without deliberate placement or special significance. It also supplies a chance baseline for interpreting apparent linear structure in computer vision and astronomy.
misconceptions: An apparent line is not, by itself, evidence of deliberate placement.
Alignment does not require exact collinearity; it depends on the chosen width.
A larger area need not mean fewer alignments, because many more point combinations become available.
